name: Metaphysical errors flowing from Aristotle's logical confusions
plain_explanation: Because Aristotle treats 'all men' as though it names a single subject, the way 'Socrates' names one, he ends up thinking a whole species like 'man' can itself be a kind of substance, and this same confusion between particulars and universals later produces the mistaken idea that a class with exactly one member is identical to that member.
precise_definition: Russell's diagnosis that Aristotle's failure to distinguish particulars from universals produced (a) the claim, in the Categories, that a species or genus can be called a 'substance' in a 'secondary' sense, and (b) the invalid inference-pattern that a predicate of a predicate (e.g., 'human' predicated of 'Greek,' which is predicated of 'Socrates') can simply be transferred to the original subject, blurring the particular/universal distinction with, Russell says, 'disastrous consequences to philosophy.'
why_it_mattered: This is Russell's central thesis for why Aristotelian logic is not merely technically flawed but philosophically damaging: formal imprecision about subjects and predicates directly generated centuries of confused metaphysics about universals, unity, and number.
historical_origin: Traced by Russell to Aristotle's own Categories, worsened by Porphyry's less cautious commentary.
examples: 'If I say "Socrates is Greek, all Greeks are human," Aristotle thinks that "human" is a predicate of "Greek"... and obviously "human" is a predicate of "Socrates"' -- but, Russell argues, 'human' is not really a predicate of 'Greek' at all in the same sense.
influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell says this 'made it impossible to have a correct theory of the number one, and led to endless bad metaphysics about unity' (via the confusion of a one-member class with its sole member).
